ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Rapid relief without inhibiting secretion

A 34-year-old woman develops occasional postprandial heartburn. A liquid containing aluminum hydroxide and magnesium hydroxide relieves her discomfort within minutes. In an isolated gastric preparation, acid secretion continues despite a rise in luminal pH. Which mechanism best explains the relief?

  1. Irreversible inhibition of parietal-cell proton pumps
  2. Competitive blockade of parietal-cell H2 receptors
  3. Inhibition of vagal acetylcholine release
  4. Formation of an adherent polymer over ulcer bases
  5. Chemical neutralization of luminal hydrogen ions
Answer and explanation

Chemical neutralization of luminal hydrogen ions

Antacids consume acid already present in the lumen; they do not need to inhibit its production.

Option explanations

Chemical neutralization of luminal hydrogen ions: The hydroxide salts buffer existing gastric acid.

Irreversible inhibition of parietal-cell proton pumps: Proton pump inhibitors suppress secretion, which continues in this experiment.

Competitive blockade of parietal-cell H2 receptors: H2 antagonists reduce histamine-mediated secretion.

Inhibition of vagal acetylcholine release: Reduced vagal signaling would reduce secretion rather than directly neutralize acid.

Formation of an adherent polymer over ulcer bases: An adherent barrier describes sucralfate, not hydroxide antacids.
